title: Cryptography
subtitle: Trust in a connected world
notes: Welcome students. Frame the subject as a way of making digital interactions trustworthy. No prerequisites or notation are needed for this opening.

title: You used it before class.
notes: Ask which action students have already taken today: opening a secure website, making a contactless payment, signing in, or installing an update. Take one or two responses. Cryptography is infrastructure, often invisible when it works.

title: Three questions behind digital trust.
notes: Define cryptography as mathematical methods for protecting information. Explain confidentiality, integrity, and authentication in everyday language. Privacy is only one goal. Cryptanalysis studies how protections can fail. No algorithms or formulas are required.

title: New tools. New ways to communicate.
notes: Keep one short historical thread from the reference: hand-written secret messages, machine-assisted military communication, then networked digital life. Enigma cryptanalysis involved Polish work and multinational Allied teams; do not attribute it to one individual. More communication and more computation changed both the need for protection and the available methods.

title: Private words. Public networks.
notes: Use an end-to-end encrypted conversation as the example. The sending device encrypts the message and the receiving device decrypts it. The service forwarding it is not intended to hold the keys needed to read its contents. This does not describe all messaging or ordinary email. Metadata, backups, and compromised endpoints are different concerns; save those distinctions for the limitations discussion if asked.

title: How do strangers trust a connection?
notes: A browser and a website can establish an authenticated, protected connection without sharing a secret beforehand. The browser verifies the named domain using its trust infrastructure. HTTPS protects the connection, not the honesty of the website operator. bank.example is a fictional reserved domain, not a live preview or recommendation. Avoid equating an old padlock icon with trustworthy content.

title: One tap. A chain of trust.
notes: Retain finance from the reference without Swift volume statistics or Singapore magnetic-stripe timelines. A contactless chip card or mobile payment credential participates in cryptographic checks that support transaction authentication and data integrity. Online banking also uses protected channels. Avoid implying every payment method uses identical mechanisms or that cryptography alone detects all fraud.

title: Your face can unlock a key.
notes: Refresh the old password/OTP/security-token discussion with passkeys. A local PIN, fingerprint, or face check can authorize the authenticator to use a credential. The site verifies cryptographic proof rather than receiving the biometric as its login credential. Passkeys may be synced; do not claim every private key can never leave its first device. The origin binding is useful against phishing, not a guarantee that an entire account or device is invulnerable.

title: Trust travels with the data.
notes: Retain the electronic-passport idea and add a familiar software-update example. A digital signature can support checks of the origin and integrity of data. A passport chip signature authenticates signed chip data; checking the holder is another step, and a signature alone is not clone detection. A signed update can still contain bugs or harmful behavior. These qualifications belong in spoken notes rather than a second warning slide.

title: Cryptography is part of the system.
notes: Retain the reference’s central limitation without requiring the 2016 Bangladesh Bank news story. Use the clearly labeled illustrative scenario: a scammer persuades someone to approve a genuine transfer. Its cryptographic checks can succeed even though the decision was manipulated. Secure devices/software, sound key handling, people, and processes also matter. An encrypted channel can reach an attacker-controlled site; endpoint compromise can expose messages before or after encryption.

title: Next: ciphers you can see inside.
notes: Bridge directly into Lecture 01. Show a glimpse of classical secret writing without teaching its rule here. MEET becomes PHHW under a shift of three; students will work through this kind of construction next. Ask how we could hide a message and how someone else might recover it. Close on curiosity, not a new list of warnings.
